description: Bit manipulation exploits binary properties (XOR self-cancellation, AND/OR masking, shifting) to solve problems in O(1) extra space or O(2^n) enumeration far faster than array/hashset approaches — a frequent optimization lever in Hard-rated problems.
important_details: XOR is its own inverse: a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a — this cancels out paired values, isolating whatever appears an odd number of times.
n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit — the basis of Brian Kernighan's bit-counting algorithm.
A bitmask of length n (0 to 2^n - 1) can represent every possible subset of an n-element set, letting you enumerate all subsets iteratively.
Combining a bitmask with DP (bitmask DP) lets you track 'which items have been used/visited' as a single integer state, common in TSP-style and assignment problems.
other_relevant_details: Recognize the pattern from small constraints like n <= 20 (hinting at 2^n bitmask enumeration), 'appears once/twice/three times', or explicit mentions of XOR/AND/OR in the problem statement.

variations.description: Use XOR's self-cancelling property to find the one element that appears an odd number of times when every other element appears an even number of times (typically twice).
important_details: XOR-ing the entire array collapses all paired duplicates to 0, leaving only the unpaired element.
For 'appears three times except one' variants, track bits via a state machine (ones/twos) or count each bit position mod 3 across all numbers.
For 'exactly two unique numbers appear once', first XOR everything to get a^b, then use the lowest set bit of that result to split the array into two groups.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n). Space: O(1) — the entire appeal versus a hashmap-based frequency count.

problems.name: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array

variations.description: Efficiently count, check, or manipulate individual set bits using shift/AND tricks like n & (n-1), n & -n, and building up a DP table of bit counts.
important_details: n & (n-1) removes the lowest set bit — repeat until n becomes 0 to count set bits in O(number of set bits).
n & -n isolates the lowest set bit — useful in Fenwick/BIT trees and for splitting XOR results into groups.
dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1) builds a full 0..n bit-count table in O(n) using previously computed results (a DP-on-bits trick).
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n) for the full table (O(log n) per single popcount query). Space: O(n) for the table, O(1) for a single count.

variations.description: Represent every possible subset of an n-element set as an integer from 0 to 2^n - 1, where bit i indicates whether element i is included — enabling exhaustive subset enumeration in O(2^n * n).
important_details: Iterate mask from 0 to (1<<n)-1; for each mask, check bit i via (mask >> i) & 1 to know if element i is in this subset.
Only feasible when n is small (typically n <= 20), since 2^n grows explosively.
Can be combined with memoization (bitmask DP) when subsets need to be revisited across different problem states.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(2^n * n). Space: O(2^n * n) to store all subsets.

problems.name: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets

variations.description: Use a bitmask as the DP state to represent 'which items/nodes have been visited or assigned so far', compressing an exponential state space into a single integer index — the standard technique for TSP-style and assignment problems.
important_details: dp[mask][i] typically means 'minimum cost to have visited exactly the set in mask, currently at node/item i'.
Transitions try adding one more unvisited bit to the mask and moving to that item, updating dp[newMask][newItem].
Time complexity is O(2^n * n^2) or O(2^n * n) depending on the transition — only tractable for n up to ~15-20.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(2^n * n^2) typical for TSP-style DP. Space: O(2^n * n).
